newsitem.title: USA: Albright rebuffs Bulgaria on NATO.
newsitem.headline: Albright rebuffs Bulgaria on NATO.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Monday rejected a suggestion by her Bulgarian counterpart that NATO designate Bulgaria as a likely candidate for future membership in the alliance.

"It is the inclination of the United States not to name other countries" for a prospective second-round of new NATO members when the alliance meets in July to issue its first round of post-Cold War membership invitations, she said.
Albright spoke at a news conference with Bulgarian Foreign Minister Nadezhda Mikaylova. They later held a working lunch.

Mikaylova said she respected President Clinton's decision announced last week to support only three countries -- Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic -- as NATO's first post-Cold War new members when alliance leaders meet in Madrid July 8-9.
But she added: "We expect that at Madrid Bulgaria should be specifically mentioned among the interested countries that the alliance would help prepare for membership."

"The U.S. declaration gives us every reason to believe that any further enlargement would provide for a geographical balance and entail equal treatment for aspiring members from the Black Sea region," she said.
Mikaylova said the "earliest possible accession to NATO" was Bulgaria's "most immediate national interest."

"Were it not to happen at Madrid, then we'd like to hear the full commitment of NATO that the future enlargement will take place in the near future," she said. "Bulgaria deserves this act of Atlantic solidarity," she added.

Albright saluted Bulgaria's advances toward democracy and a free market economy but, in addition to rebuffing the call to name potential second-round candidates for enlargement, she did not commit herself to a specific date when a second round of new NATO members would be taken in.
Albright did however repeat the strong U.S. position that the door wil remain open for other members in the future.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said later that there is a consensu in NATO for a second round of expansion but "we've not actually established a date for it yet."

"But you can be assured that when the president of the United States and the secretary of state both say that the United States wants this to happen, it's a fairly good bet that we're going to use all the influence we can bring to bear in NATO to make sure that happens," he said.
Burns described Bulgaria as among the "future possible candidates" and said the United States hoped that "it can one day...become a totally, seriously viable candidate for NATO membership."
